pages.text: On summer evenings, Leo stayed at Grandpa’s house in the village. From the kitchen, Leo called, “Grandpa, do you want some lemonade?” From the porch, Grandpa called back, “Lemons? No, the lemons aren’t ripe yet!”

pages.text: Leo rolled his eyes. “Never mind!” he shouted. Grandpa went quiet. He turned his chair towards the hills and looked at them for a long time. Leo poured the lemonade himself. The ice cubes clinked very loudly in the glasses.

pages.text: After supper, the cousins came. Everybody sat on the porch while the sun went down behind the hills. The cicadas sang. The cousins talked fast, all at once, and laughed at everything. It was the noisiest porch in the whole village.
pages.speech: After supper, the cousins came. Everybody sat on the porch while the sun went down behind the hills. The cicadas sang. The cousins talked fast, all at once, and laughed at everything. It was the noisiest porch in the whole village.

pages.text: Then the big cousin told a riddle. Everyone laughed, and Grandpa laughed too, a little late. It was a small, careful laugh. Then he looked back at the hills. Leo watched Grandpa’s face. He didn’t hear it, Leo thought.

pages.text: Leo remembered how he had shouted “Never mind!” from the kitchen. His cheeks went hot. Grandpa hadn’t answered the wrong question on purpose. He just couldn’t hear Leo from so far away, across the yard and over the cicadas.

pages.text: Leo picked up his chair and carried it across the porch. He put it down right in front of Grandpa, so close that their knees almost touched. Face to face. Grandpa looked surprised. Then his eyebrows lifted, and he waited.
pages.speech: Leo picked up his chair and carried it across the porch. He put it down right in front of Grandpa, so close that their knees almost touched. Face to face. Grandpa looked surprised. Then his eyebrows lifted, and he waited.

pages.text: “Grandpa,” said Leo slowly and clearly. Not loudly, just clearly. “Do you want to hear the riddle?” Grandpa watched Leo’s mouth and nodded. “Yes, please.” The cousins stopped talking. Even the cicadas seemed to listen.
pages.speech: “Grandpa,” said Leo slowly and clearly. Not loudly, just clearly. “Do you want to hear the riddle?” Grandpa watched Leo’s mouth and nodded. “Yes, please.” The cousins stopped talking. Even the cicadas seemed to listen.

pages.text: “What has a neck but no head?” asked Leo. Grandpa frowned. “A what? A deck?” Leo didn’t shout it again. He touched his own neck with two fingers. “A neck,” he said. “Like this.”

pages.text: Grandpa’s eyes began to shine. “A neck, but no head,” he said slowly, thinking. Leo drew a shape in the air with both hands, round at the bottom and thin at the top. Then he pretended to drink from it.

pages.text: “A bottle!” cried Grandpa. And he laughed. This time it was a big laugh. It rolled off the porch and all the way down to the hills. The cousins laughed with him, and the little cousin laughed loudest of all.
pages.speech: “A bottle!” cried Grandpa. And he laughed. This time it was a big laugh. It rolled off the porch and all the way down to the hills. The cousins laughed with him, and the little cousin laughed loudest of all.

pages.text: The little cousin dragged his chair over too. So did the big cousin. Soon they all sat close to Grandpa, face to face, and nobody talked at once any more. When Grandpa missed a word, someone said it another way.
pages.speech: The little cousin dragged his chair over too. So did the big cousin. Soon they all sat close to Grandpa, face to face, and nobody talked at once any more. When Grandpa missed a word, someone said it another way.

pages.text: “Now I have one for you,” said Grandpa. “From when I was a shepherd boy in these hills.” He leaned in. Everyone leaned in. Leo’s heart gave a happy jump. Grandpa had stories, and Leo had almost missed them.
pages.speech: “Now I have one for you,” said Grandpa. “From when I was a shepherd boy in these hills.” He leaned in. Everyone leaned in. Leo’s heart gave a happy jump. Grandpa had stories, and Leo had almost missed them.

pages.text: “I had thirty goats,” said Grandpa, “and every evening they refused to come home. So I sang to them. But my voice was so terrible that all thirty goats ran home as fast as they could. They just wanted to get away from it!”

pages.text: The cousins laughed so hard they nearly fell off their chairs. Grandpa told another story, and another, until the stars came out over the hills. And all evening long, Leo kept his chair just where it was, face to face.

activity.title: Silent Messages
activity.goal: Communicate without sound, using face, lips and hands.
materials: A sheet of paper and a pencil (optional, to mark the easy words)

steps.caption: Sit face to face, close together.
Say a word with no sound. Use your lips, face and hands.
Which words were easy? Tick them.

activity.safety: There are no materials to worry about. Sit in good light so that faces are easy to see. If a child or an adult in the group has a hearing loss, ask them how they like to communicate and follow their lead. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Leo’s grandfather hears less than he used to. Leo learns what hearing specialists advise: come close, face the person, make sure the light is on your face, speak clearly and a little slower without shouting, cut the background noise, and when a word is missed, say it another way instead of repeating it louder. This game lets children feel how much a face, lips and hands can say. Sit face to face, close, in good light. One person says a word with no sound at all, using lips, face and hands; the other guesses. Start with easy words such as “cat”, “water” and “sleep”, then swap. Before each new word, ask the child to predict: “Will this one be easy or hard to guess?” Afterwards, tick the easy words on the paper and talk about why they were easy. Usually the words that can be shown with the hands win. Then try short sentences, such as “I am hungry” or “Where is the ball?” Praise the effort to be understood (“you found another way to show it”), not who guessed the most. Twenty minutes is about right. To make it easier, use only words that can be acted out. To make it harder, use words without an action, such as “yesterday” or “blue”, and find another way to show them. If a grandparent joins in, let them choose the words.
activity.inClass: Pairs sit face to face and take turns, three words each, then swap partners. Then one child at a time stands in front of the class and “says” a word with no sound while the class guesses. The teacher keeps a short list on the board of the words that were easiest to guess, and asks the class what made them easy.
